Pida a los estudiantes que relaten un malentendido intercultural vivido o conocido. Pregunta: Have you ever said ‘yes’ when you meant ‘maybe’? What could happen in an international team?

slides.title: Listening strategies for meetings
bullets: Before: read the agenda, predict vocabulary and prepare one question.
During: focus on key words, numbers and names; don't translate every word.
Use captions and transcripts when available, but verify numbers and names.
After: compare notes with a colleague and send a recap.
slides.notes: Cierre la unidad con estrategias de comprensión auditiva, la habilidad que más preocupa a los estudiantes. Explique que nadie entiende el cien por ciento en una segunda lengua; el objetivo es captar el propósito, las cifras y los acuerdos. La preparación previa con la agenda reduce la carga cognitiva. Recomiende no traducir mentalmente palabra por palabra, porque se pierde el hilo. Mencione que los subtítulos automáticos de las plataformas ayudan, pero se equivocan con nombres propios y cifras. Actividad: escuchar un audio de reunión de dos minutos con una ficha de predicción previa y una de verificación posterior. Pregunta: What percentage of the audio did you understand, and was it enough to complete the task? Discuta la diferencia entre comprensión total y suficiente.

reading.title: Speaking Up in Virtual Meetings: Language, Numbers and Culture
reading.content:
## The meeting is the workplace

For many remote professionals, the meeting is the main place where they are seen. Decisions are made, tasks are assigned and impressions are formed in calls on Zoom, Teams or Google Meet. If you stay silent, your colleagues may think you have nothing to contribute, even if your work is excellent. This reading presents practical language and strategies to participate actively, even at A2+/B1 level.

## Strategic competence: the power of clarifying

The CEFR Companion Volume (Council of Europe, 2020) includes *asking for clarification* as part of interaction competence. Successful second-language speakers are not the ones who understand everything; they are the ones who **manage** what they don't understand. Useful phrases include:

- *"Sorry, could you repeat the last part?"*
- *"What do you mean by 'scope'?"*
- *"So, if I understand correctly, the deadline is Monday, not Friday?"*

Paraphrasing what you heard is particularly powerful: it confirms understanding and shows active listening.

## Numbers without mistakes

Numbers cause many costly errors. Three rules help:

1. **Separators:** in English, the comma separates thousands and the point marks decimals. *1,250.50* is "one thousand, two hundred and fifty point five zero". In Peru, the same amount is often written *1 250,50*.
2. **Stress:** *thirTEEN, fourTEEN, fifTEEN* have stress at the end; *THIRty, FORty, FIFty* at the beginning. If in doubt, say the digits: "one-five".
3. **Confirmation:** repeat important figures and confirm them in writing.

## Describing trends

Reports often describe changes over time. Look at this example from a marketing dashboard:

> *Instagram engagement **rose sharply** from 2.1% in January to 4.8% in March, after the launch of short videos. It then **fell slightly** to 4.3% in April and **remained stable** in May.*

Notice the structure: verb + adverb + *from... to...*. Use *by* for the size of the change: *"Sales increased by 12%."* Use *at* for a level: *"The rate stood at 4.3%."* Remember the irregular past forms: *rise – rose*, *fall – fell*, *grow – grew*.

## Comparing and recommending

Decisions need comparisons: *"Supplier A is cheaper than Supplier B, but B is much more reliable."* Modifiers like *much, slightly* and *a bit* make your comparison precise. A professional comparison ends with a recommendation: *"So I recommend Supplier B, because a delay would cost more than the price difference."*

## Talking about the future

Meetings end with commitments, so future forms are essential:

| Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *will* | spontaneous decisions, promises | *"I'll send the file after the call."* |
| *going to* | plans already decided | *"We're going to migrate the server in July."* |
| present continuous | fixed arrangements | *"I'm meeting the auditor on Thursday."* |

## Culture: high and low context

The anthropologist Edward T. Hall described **high-context** cultures, where much meaning is implicit, and **low-context** cultures, where meaning is stated explicitly. Erin Meyer's *The Culture Map* (2014) developed these ideas into eight scales, including how people communicate, give negative feedback, disagree and treat time.

Peruvian professional culture tends to be relatively high-context and indirect: we may say *"I'll try"* or *"let me see"* to avoid a direct *no*. A colleague from the United States, the Netherlands or Germany may interpret these phrases differently. A useful rule for international teams is: **be more explicit than you would be in Spanish**. Instead of *"Maybe it will be difficult"*, say *"I can't finish it by Friday. I can deliver it on Tuesday."*

Avoid stereotypes, however. Scales are relative, and individuals vary. The goal is not to label people but to anticipate misunderstandings.

## Minutes and recaps

At the end of a meeting, someone should record **decisions** and **action items**. A good action item has three elements: who, what and when: *"Luis will send the revised quote by Friday, June 6."* A recap email within 24 hours confirms understanding and creates a written record, which is especially useful when the team works in a second language.

## Conclusion

Participation in meetings is a skill you can train. Prepare one contribution before each call, use clarifying phrases without fear, check numbers twice and confirm agreements in writing. Your English does not need to be perfect to be effective; it needs to be clear, explicit and well-timed.

case.title: Caso: The silent analyst at DataPacífico
case.content:
**DataPacífico** is a data and software services company based in San Isidro, Lima, with 70 employees. Since 2024, it has worked for **ShopWave**, an e-commerce company in Miami, providing weekly sales dashboards and a demand forecasting model. The contract is worth US$ 15,000 per month and is renewed every quarter.

Every Tuesday at 10:00 a.m. Lima time, there is a 30-minute video call with ShopWave's operations director, **Mike Brennan**, and two analysts from India who also work for ShopWave. DataPacífico sends **Sofía Huamán**, a junior data analyst, and her supervisor, **Andrés Cárdenas**, who speaks fluent English.

Sofía built most of the forecasting model and understands the data better than anyone. However, in the meetings she rarely speaks. Andrés presents her results, sometimes with small errors. Last week, three problems happened:

1. Mike asked whether returns in April were **"fifteen or fifty percent higher"** than in March. Andrés said "fifty", but the real figure was 15%. Mike sent an alarmed email to ShopWave's CEO before the error was corrected.
2. One of the Indian analysts, **Priya**, proposed changing the forecasting horizon from four to eight weeks. Sofía knew this would reduce accuracy from about 91% to 84%, but she said nothing. Andrés answered, *"Yes, we'll try."* Mike understood it as a firm commitment for the next sprint.
3. Nobody sent minutes. Two days later, each team had a different understanding of the deadlines.

Andrés's manager, **Gabriela Ríos**, reviewed the situation. She knows that ShopWave is evaluating whether to renew the contract in six weeks and that a competitor in Colombia offers a similar service. She is considering three actions: (a) ask Sofía to present her own results every week, with preparation support; (b) keep Andrés as the only speaker but require written confirmation of all figures; (c) introduce a standard meeting protocol: agenda sent 24 hours before, a numbers check, explicit answers to proposals and minutes within two hours.

Sofía told Gabriela privately: *"My English is not good enough. I understand almost everything, but I'm afraid of making mistakes in front of the client."* Her last internal test placed her at A2+ in speaking and B1 in listening and reading.

Gabriela must decide what to do before next Tuesday.
questions: Explain each of the three problems using concepts from the unit: numbers and stress, high- and low-context communication, and minutes.
How should Andrés or Sofía have responded to Priya's proposal? Write an explicit and polite answer of three or four sentences.
Evaluate Gabriela's three options. Could they be combined? Which would best protect the contract and develop Sofía?
Design a two-week preparation plan for Sofía to present the forecasting results in English. Include specific phrases she should practice.

assignment.title: Simulación de reunión virtual y acta en inglés
assignment.instructions:
**Objetivo:** participar eficazmente en una reunión virtual en inglés y registrar sus acuerdos.

**Modalidad:** trabajo en tríos (de preferencia, de carreras distintas).

**Qué entregar:**

1. **Grabación de una reunión de 8 a 10 minutos** sobre un problema de su campo: por ejemplo, elegir entre tres proveedores, decidir cómo responder a una caída de ventas o priorizar mejoras de un sistema. Cada participante debe: (a) abrir o cerrar una parte de la reunión; (b) presentar al menos un dato numérico o una tendencia usando el vocabulario de la unidad; (c) comparar opciones; (d) pedir una aclaración; (e) expresar acuerdo y desacuerdo cortés; (f) asumir un compromiso con *will* o *going to*.
2. **Acta en inglés** (150 a 220 palabras): fecha, asistentes, decisiones (pasado simple) y acciones con responsable y plazo.
3. **Correo de resumen** (80 a 120 palabras) enviado al cliente o jefe ficticio.
4. **Autoevaluación individual en español** (máximo 120 palabras): qué estrategias de aclaración usaste y qué mejorarías.

**Formato:** grabación desde la plataforma de videoconferencia con cámaras encendidas; documentos en PDF. Se permite usar notas breves, no guiones leídos.

**Criterios:** rúbrica adjunta; la calificación de interacción es individual.

rubric.name: Interacción: turnos, aclaraciones, acuerdo y desacuerdo cortés
Uso preciso de cifras, tendencias y comparaciones
Formas de futuro y compromisos explícitos
Acta y correo de resumen claros y completos

questions.prompt: During a call, you didn't understand the deadline the client mentioned. What is the best strategy?
options: Say ‘OK’ and ask a colleague later.
Say ‘Sorry, could you repeat the deadline, please?’ and confirm it.
Guess the most probable date.
Wait for the client to send an email.
questions.explanation: Pedir repetición y confirmar es una estrategia de interacción profesional; fingir comprensión o suponer genera errores costosos.

questions.prompt: How do you read the figure US$ 1,250.75 in English?
options: One point two five zero comma seventy-five dollars
One thousand, two hundred and fifty dollars and seventy-five cents
One million two hundred fifty thousand seventy-five dollars
Twelve fifty point seventy-five thousand dollars
questions.explanation: En inglés la coma separa los miles y el punto marca los decimales, que en dinero se leen como centavos.

questions.prompt: Sales were 200 units in May and 230 in June. Which sentence describes the change correctly?
options: Sales increased by 15% from May to June.
Sales increased at 15% in June.
Sales increased from 15% to 230 units.
Sales fell by 30 units in June.
questions.explanation: El aumento fue de 30 unidades sobre 200, es decir, 15%; ‘by’ expresa la magnitud del cambio.

questions.prompt: In a meeting, your manager asks: ‘Who can send the updated budget?’ What is the most natural answer?
options: I'm going to send it, I decided last month.
I send it.
I'll send it after the call.
I am sending it last week.
questions.explanation: Para una decisión espontánea o un ofrecimiento en el momento se usa ‘will’; ‘going to’ indica un plan previo.

questions.prompt: A colleague proposes an idea you think is risky. Which reply is polite and explicit?
options: No, that's wrong.
Maybe, we'll see, I'll try.
I see your point, but I'm worried it will reduce accuracy from 91% to 84%.
Yes, perfect, excellent idea.
questions.explanation: Combina reconocimiento, desacuerdo explícito y un dato; ‘we'll try’ es ambiguo en culturas de bajo contexto.

questions.prompt: Which action item is written correctly for meeting minutes?
options: Send quote.
Somebody should send the quote soon.
Luis will send the revised quote to ShopWave by Friday, June 6.
The quote was a topic of the meeting.
questions.explanation: Un buen ítem de acción indica responsable, acción concreta y plazo; las otras opciones omiten al menos uno de estos elementos.

questions.prompt: According to Hall and Meyer, what is a useful strategy for a Peruvian professional working with a low-context team?
options: Use indirect phrases to avoid conflict.
Be more explicit than usual and confirm agreements in writing.
Never disagree with clients.
Speak only when asked a direct question.
questions.explanation: En culturas de bajo contexto el significado se espera explícito; ser claro y confirmar por escrito reduce malentendidos.

units.title: Unidad 4 · Integrating skills: processes, presentations and job interviews
units.description: El estudiante integra las competencias del curso para describir procesos de su área, presentar su trabajo con apoyo visual, redactar un currículum y una carta de presentación en inglés y desempeñarse en una entrevista laboral simulada usando el método STAR.
topics: Describing processes with sequencers and the present simple passive
Short presentations: structure, signposting, visuals and Q&A
Talking about experience with the present perfect
CV and cover letter in English
Job interviews and the STAR method

slides.title: Describing a process step by step
bullets: Sequencers: first, then, next, after that, once…, finally.
Purpose and result: ‘in order to…’, ‘so that…’, ‘as a result…’.
Example: ‘First, the invoice is received. Then it's checked against the purchase order. Finally, it's approved for payment.’
Choose the right level of detail for your audience: a client needs the big picture; a new colleague needs every step.
slides.notes: Inicie la unidad integradora explicando que describir procesos es una de las tareas más frecuentes del trabajo: capacitar a un compañero, explicar a un cliente cómo funciona un servicio, documentar un procedimiento. Conecte con los procesos de cada carrera: ciclo de cuentas por pagar, flujo de producción de una pieza gráfica, atención de un ticket de soporte, ciclo de una campaña digital, flujo de entrenamiento de un modelo. Muestre un diagrama de flujo simple y modele su descripción con secuenciadores. Actividad: en parejas, cada estudiante describe un proceso de su área en seis pasos y el compañero lo dibuja como diagrama; luego se compara con el original. Pregunta: Was your partner's diagram the same as your process? If not, which step was unclear?

slides.title: The present simple passive for processes
bullets: Form: am/is/are + past participle: ‘The data is cleaned and then it's loaded into the database.’
Use: when the action matters more than the person who does it.
Add the agent with ‘by’ only if it is important: ‘The payment is approved by the finance manager.’
Common participles: checked, sent, approved, designed, printed, tested, deployed, recorded.
slides.notes: Presente la voz pasiva como herramienta funcional, no como transformación mecánica. En la descripción de procesos lo importante es qué ocurre con el objeto (la factura, el diseño, el código), no quién lo hace. Contraste con la unidad 2, donde recomendamos voz activa para asignar responsabilidades en correos: ambas tienen su lugar. Practique con participios irregulares frecuentes: sent, made, written, paid, built. Señale el error ‘is send’ (debe ser ‘is sent’). Actividad: transformar una descripción en voz activa de un proceso contable o de despliegue de software en voz pasiva y discutir cuál versión es más adecuada para un manual. Pregunta: When is it important to say who does the action? Respuesta: en controles, aprobaciones y responsabilidades legales.

slides.title: Writing clear instructions
bullets: Use imperatives for steps: ‘Open the file. Click Export. Select PDF.’
One action per step; number the steps; add warnings: ‘Make sure you save a backup first.’
Negative imperatives: ‘Don't close the window during the update.’
Test your instructions with someone who doesn't know the task.
slides.notes: Las instrucciones son un género distinto de la descripción de procesos: se dirigen a quien ejecuta la tarea. Muestre ejemplos de manuales de software, guías de estilo de marca y procedimientos de oficina. Explique el imperativo, la estructura más simple del inglés, y la fórmula ‘Make sure you…’ para advertencias. Comente que la documentación técnica en inglés de herramientas como Excel, Figma o Python sigue este estilo y que leerla es una excelente práctica. Actividad: cada estudiante redacta instrucciones de cinco pasos para una tarea de su carrera, como exportar un archivo para imprenta, generar un reporte en un sistema contable o reiniciar un servicio; un compañero intenta seguirlas sin preguntar. Pregunta: Which step caused confusion, and how would you rewrite it?

slides.title: Structuring a short presentation
bullets: Introduction: greet, topic, purpose, outline: ‘Today I'm going to talk about… I'll cover three points.’
Body: three main points maximum, each with one example or data point.
Conclusion: summary and call to action: ‘To sum up… I'd recommend…’
Timing: about 120–130 words per minute for clear second-language speech.
slides.notes: Retome la estructura de presentación trabajada en Comunicación Efectiva y adáptela al inglés. Explique la regla de tres puntos principales como máximo, sobre todo en una segunda lengua y en formato virtual. Muestre cómo calcular la extensión: una presentación de tres minutos equivale a unas 360 a 400 palabras pronunciadas con calma. Advierta contra leer las diapositivas o un guion completo; recomiende notas con palabras clave. Modele una apertura de 30 segundos sobre un proyecto académico. Actividad: cada estudiante prepara el esquema de una presentación de tres minutos sobre un proceso o proyecto de su carrera, que será base del proyecto final. Pregunta: How do you keep the audience's attention in an online presentation? Recoja ideas: preguntas, datos, ejemplos.

slides.title: Signposting language
bullets: Moving on: ‘Let's move on to…’ ‘Now I'd like to look at…’
Adding and contrasting: ‘In addition…’ ‘However…’ ‘On the other hand…’
Giving examples: ‘For example…’ ‘Let me give you an example.’
Concluding: ‘To sum up…’ ‘The key takeaway is…’ ‘Thank you. I'm happy to take questions.’
slides.notes: Las señales discursivas son el mapa que ayuda a la audiencia a seguir la presentación, especialmente cuando se escucha en una segunda lengua. Explique que también ayudan al presentador: si olvida una idea, la señal le da tiempo y estructura. Haga una práctica coral con las frases más útiles y luego un ejercicio en cadena: cada estudiante dice una oración de transición para pasar de un punto a otro en un tema común. Señale la entonación: las transiciones se marcan con una breve pausa antes y después. Conecte con la redacción del acta y del correo, donde los conectores cumplen la misma función. Pregunta: Which signposting phrases do you use in Spanish presentations, and what are their English equivalents?

slides.title: Presenting visuals and data
bullets: Introduce the visual: ‘This chart shows… The vertical axis represents…’
Highlight the key point: ‘As you can see, costs dropped significantly in Q2.’
Explain the cause or implication: ‘This was mainly due to… This means that…’
Keep slides simple: one message per slide, readable fonts, few words.
slides.notes: Integre el vocabulario de tendencias de la unidad 3 con la presentación de material visual. Explique la secuencia de tres pasos: presentar el gráfico, destacar el dato clave y explicar la causa o implicancia. Muestre un gráfico real de tipo general, como la evolución mensual de un indicador o las ventas de una empresa ficticia, y modele la explicación. Para Diseño Gráfico, enfatice la relación entre diseño de la diapositiva y mensaje; para Computación e IA, la explicación de métricas de un sistema o modelo. Recuerde el principio de una idea por diapositiva. Actividad: cada estudiante presenta en 45 segundos un gráfico asignado. Pregunta: What's the difference between describing a chart and interpreting it? La interpretación responde a ‘so what?’.

slides.title: Handling questions after a presentation
bullets: Welcome the question: ‘Thanks, that's a good question.’
Clarify if needed: ‘Just to make sure I understand, are you asking about cost or time?’
If you don't know: ‘I don't have that figure right now, but I'll check and send it to you today.’
Bridge back to your message: ‘That's why we recommend option B.’
slides.notes: La ronda de preguntas genera ansiedad porque no se puede preparar por completo. Explique que sí se pueden preparar estrategias: agradecer, aclarar, responder brevemente y volver al mensaje principal. Destaque la honestidad: decir que no se tiene un dato y comprometerse a enviarlo es profesional; inventar una respuesta es arriesgado. Practique la técnica de parafrasear la pregunta, que da tiempo para pensar y verifica la comprensión. Actividad: tras las presentaciones de 45 segundos, dos compañeros hacen preguntas y el presentador aplica las estrategias. El docente anota frases bien usadas. Pregunta: What would you do if a client asks a question you don't understand at all? Respuesta esperada: pedir que reformule o dé un ejemplo.

slides.title: Talking about experience: present perfect
bullets: Form: have/has + past participle: ‘I've worked with Excel for three years.’
For (duration) vs since (starting point): for two years / since 2024.
Experience without a specific time: ‘I've designed logos for five local businesses.’
Past simple for specific times: ‘In 2025, I completed an internship at a logistics company.’
slides.notes: El presente perfecto es central en entrevistas y currículums. Explique su uso para experiencias hasta el presente y su contraste con el pasado simple, que requiere un momento terminado. Error típico de hispanohablantes: ‘I work here since 2024’ en lugar de ‘I've worked here since 2024’. Practique ‘for’ y ‘since’ con datos propios de los estudiantes. Como muchos aún no tienen experiencia laboral formal, muestre cómo valorar la experiencia académica, de voluntariado o de emprendimiento familiar: ‘I've managed the social media accounts of my family's restaurant for a year.’ Actividad: cada estudiante escribe cinco oraciones sobre su experiencia combinando presente perfecto y pasado simple. Pregunta: How long have you studied at TEPSUP, and what have you learned so far?

slides.title: The CV in English: key differences
bullets: Usually no photo, age, marital status or national ID number, especially for US and UK employers.
Reverse chronological order; one or two pages; consistent format.
Bullet points starting with action verbs: managed, designed, developed, reduced, improved.
Quantify achievements: ‘Reduced invoice processing time by 20%.’ ‘Designed 30 posts per month.’
slides.notes: Explique las diferencias culturales del currículum: en el Perú es común incluir foto, DNI y estado civil, mientras que en Estados Unidos y el Reino Unido se omiten para prevenir discriminación. Advierta que las convenciones varían según el país y la empresa, por lo que conviene revisar la oferta. Muestre la estructura: datos de contacto, perfil breve, experiencia, educación, habilidades e idiomas. Enfatice los verbos de acción y la cuantificación de logros, que transforman tareas en resultados. Indique cómo describir el nivel de idioma con el MCER (‘English: B1, CEFR’) y no con términos vagos como ‘intermediate’. Actividad: convertir tres funciones vagas en logros cuantificados. Pregunta: What is the difference between a responsibility and an achievement on a CV?

slides.title: The cover letter
bullets: Paragraph 1: the position and how you found it: ‘I'm writing to apply for the Junior Data Analyst position…’
Paragraph 2: why you are a good fit: two or three skills with evidence.
Paragraph 3: why this company: show you researched it.
Paragraph 4: call to action: ‘I would welcome the opportunity to discuss…’
slides.notes: La carta de presentación sigue usándose en muchas convocatorias internacionales y en plataformas de trabajo remoto. Presente la estructura de cuatro párrafos y relacione con lo aprendido en correos: propósito al inicio, evidencia en el cuerpo y llamada a la acción al final. Insista en personalizar la carta: una carta genérica se detecta de inmediato. Explique cómo mostrar que se investigó a la empresa mencionando un proyecto, producto o valor concreto. Advierta sobre el uso de inteligencia artificial: las cartas generadas sin edición suenan genéricas y pueden contener afirmaciones falsas. Actividad: analizar una oferta laboral real de tipo junior en inglés y extraer palabras clave para la carta. Pregunta: How can you show motivation without using clichés like ‘I'm passionate’?

slides.title: Common interview questions
bullets: ‘Tell me about yourself.’ – use your professional introduction from Unit 1, updated.
‘What are your strengths and weaknesses?’ – give evidence; show how you work on a weakness.
‘Why do you want to work here?’ – connect your goals with the company's needs.
‘Where do you see yourself in five years?’ – realistic growth linked to the role.
slides.notes: Explique que la entrevista en inglés reutiliza todo lo aprendido: presentación personal, presente simple y continuo, pasado, futuro y presente perfecto. Muestre que la pregunta ‘Tell me about yourself’ no pide la biografía completa, sino un resumen profesional de 60 a 90 segundos, la evolución del video de la unidad 1. Para la pregunta de debilidades, explique la estrategia de mencionar una debilidad real, no crítica para el puesto, y lo que se hace para mejorarla. Practique en parejas con preguntas aleatorias y un minuto por respuesta. Señale que en entrevistas remotas hay que cuidar el entorno, la cámara y la conexión. Pregunta: What is a real weakness you could mention honestly, and how are you working on it?

slides.title: The STAR method for behavioral questions
bullets: Behavioral questions: ‘Tell me about a time when you solved a problem / worked in a team / met a tight deadline.’
Situation: context in one or two sentences (past simple).
Task: your responsibility; Action: what YOU did, step by step (use ‘I’, not only ‘we’).
Result: measurable outcome and what you learned: ‘As a result, we delivered two days early.’
slides.notes: El método STAR es el estándar para responder preguntas conductuales, muy usadas por empresas multinacionales porque el comportamiento pasado predice el futuro. Explique cada componente y la proporción recomendada: situación y tarea breves, acción como parte principal, resultado concreto. Señale el error de hablar solo en plural: el entrevistador quiere saber qué hizo el candidato. Modele una respuesta de 90 segundos basada en una experiencia académica: un proyecto de base de datos con plazo ajustado o una campaña para un emprendimiento local. Actividad: cada estudiante prepara dos historias STAR sobre trabajo en equipo y resolución de problemas. Pregunta: Why do interviewers prefer stories to general statements like ‘I'm a team player’?

slides.title: Practical questions and asking the interviewer
bullets: Availability: ‘I'm available to start on March 1.’ ‘I can work full time, Monday to Friday.’
Remote work: ‘I have a stable connection and a quiet workspace; I'm in Lima, UTC-5.’
Salary: ‘Based on my research, I'd expect a range of… but I'm open to discussing it.’
Your questions: ‘What does a typical day look like?’ ‘How do you measure success in this role?’
slides.notes: Prepare a los estudiantes para preguntas prácticas que suelen tomarlos por sorpresa: disponibilidad, zona horaria, equipo y conexión para trabajo remoto, expectativas salariales. Explique que conviene investigar rangos salariales del mercado y dar un rango, mostrando apertura. Destaque que al final casi siempre se pregunta ‘Do you have any questions for us?’ y que responder ‘No’ transmite poco interés. Proponga preguntas inteligentes sobre el rol, el equipo y los criterios de éxito, y desaconseje preguntar por vacaciones en la primera entrevista. Actividad: cada estudiante redacta tres preguntas para el entrevistador adaptadas a una oferta real. Pregunta: What question would show that you researched the company? Comparta ejemplos destacados en la plenaria.

slides.title: Final project: bilingual professional portfolio
bullets: CV in English (one page) and cover letter for a real junior job ad in your field.
Three-minute recorded presentation of a process or project from your career, with visuals.
Live mock interview (10 minutes) with at least one STAR answer.
Reflection: progress against CEFR descriptors since week 1, with evidence from your portfolio.
slides.notes: Presente el proyecto final como integración de las cuatro unidades. Explique que el portafolio tiene doble valor: es evidencia de aprendizaje para la calificación y un recurso real para postular a prácticas preprofesionales y empleos. Revise los componentes y su relación con cada unidad: identidad profesional, comunicación escrita, interacción oral y la integración final. Indique el cronograma de las semanas 13 a 16, con entregas parciales y retroalimentación antes de la entrevista simulada. Aclare los criterios de evaluación y muestre un ejemplo de portafolio de un ciclo anterior, si existe, o un modelo elaborado por el docente. Pregunta: Which job ad will you choose for your final project, and why? Pida que la compartan en el foro esta semana.

slides.title: Self-assessment and next steps toward B1
bullets: Compare your week 1 and week 13 recordings: fluency, accuracy, vocabulary, confidence.
Update your CEFR can-do checklist with evidence for each descriptor.
Inglés para el Trabajo II will focus on negotiations, reports and more complex grammar.
Keep a routine: 20 minutes a day of reading, listening or speaking in your field.
slides.notes: Cierre el curso con una reflexión metacognitiva. Pida a los estudiantes comparar la grabación de su presentación de la semana 1 con una grabación actual y anotar tres mejoras concretas y dos aspectos por trabajar. Actualizar la lista de descriptores con evidencias convierte la autoevaluación en algo verificable. Anticipe los contenidos de Inglés para el Trabajo II en el siguiente ciclo para dar continuidad. Insista en que el aprendizaje de idiomas depende de la exposición sostenida: veinte minutos diarios valen más que tres horas una vez por semana. Sugiera fuentes según la carrera. Pregunta final: What is one thing you can do in English now that you couldn't do in week 1? Recoja respuestas como cierre motivador del ciclo.

reading.title: From Process to Pitch: Presenting Your Work and Yourself
reading.content:
## Integration: putting the pieces together

In the first three units, you learned to introduce yourself, write professional emails and participate in meetings. This final unit integrates those skills in three high-stakes situations: **explaining how work is done**, **presenting results** and **getting a job**. In all three, the same principle applies: a clear structure makes limited language powerful.

## Describing processes

A process description explains a sequence of actions. Two tools are essential: **sequencers** (*first, then, next, after that, finally*) and the **present simple passive**. The passive is used when the action matters more than the person who does it. Compare a description of an accounts payable process:

> *First, the supplier's invoice **is received** by email. Then it **is checked** against the purchase order and the delivery note. If the three documents match, the invoice **is recorded** in the accounting system and **approved** by the finance manager. Finally, the payment **is made** by bank transfer on the scheduled date.*

The passive is formed with *am/is/are* + past participle. Learn the irregular participles you will need: *sent, made, paid, written, built*. Add the agent with *by* only when it matters, for example, in approvals and controls.

The same pattern works in any field. A developer might write: *"The code is reviewed, tested automatically and then deployed to the production server."* A designer: *"The concept is presented to the client, adjusted after feedback and finally prepared for print."*

## Presenting your work

A short professional presentation has three parts: an **introduction** with purpose and outline, a **body** with no more than three main points, and a **conclusion** with a summary and a recommendation. Signposting phrases guide the listener: *"Let's move on to..."*, *"However..."*, *"To sum up..."*.

When you present a chart, follow three steps: **introduce** it (*"This chart shows monthly support tickets in 2025"*), **highlight** the key point (*"As you can see, tickets dropped by 35% after we launched the self-service portal"*) and **interpret** it (*"This means the team can spend more time on complex problems"*). The interpretation answers the question every audience asks: *so what?*

For a second-language speaker, a pace of about 120 to 130 words per minute is clear and comfortable. A three-minute presentation therefore needs about 360 to 400 words. Use notes with key words, not a full script.

## Talking about your experience

Interviews and CVs require the **present perfect** to talk about experience connected to the present: *"I've worked with Excel for three years." "I've designed logos for five local businesses."* Use **for** with a duration and **since** with a starting point. When you mention a specific finished time, switch to the past simple: *"In 2025, I completed an internship at a logistics company in Callao."* A common error for Spanish speakers is *"I work here since 2024"*; the correct form is *"I've worked here since 2024."*

## The CV and the cover letter

International CVs follow different conventions from many Peruvian ones. For employers in the United States and the United Kingdom, CVs usually omit photos, age, marital status and ID numbers. They use reverse chronological order and **bullet points that start with action verbs** and show results: *"Reduced invoice processing time by 20% by creating an Excel template."* Language level should be expressed with the CEFR: *"English – B1 (CEFR)"*.

A cover letter usually has four paragraphs: the position, your fit (with evidence), your interest in the company (showing research) and a call to action.

## The job interview and the STAR method

Many companies use **behavioral questions**: *"Tell me about a time when you had to meet a tight deadline."* The STAR method organizes an effective answer:

- **Situation**: *"In my second semester, our team had to deliver a database project for a local bakery in two weeks."*
- **Task**: *"I was responsible for designing the tables and the sales report."*
- **Action**: *"I divided the work into daily goals, created a shared checklist and met the owner twice to validate requirements."*
- **Result**: *"We delivered two days early, and the bakery now uses the report every week. I learned to validate requirements early."*

Notice the tenses: past simple for the story, and *I* rather than *we* for your actions. Interviewers want evidence, not adjectives.

## Conclusion

The final project of this course asks you to build a bilingual professional portfolio: a CV, a cover letter, a recorded presentation and a mock interview. These are not only academic products; they are tools you can use next semester to apply for pre-professional internships. Structure, evidence and clarity will carry your message, even when your grammar is still developing.

case.title: Caso: Two candidates for a remote role at NorthBridge Software
case.content:
**NorthBridge Software** is a Canadian company based in Toronto that develops cloud accounting and invoicing tools for small businesses. It has 220 employees and is expanding its customer support and operations team in Latin America. Through **Talento Remoto Perú**, a Lima-based recruitment firm, it opened a position for a **Junior Operations & Support Analyst**: full time, remote from Peru, working hours 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Toronto time, monthly salary between US$ 1,100 and 1,400. Requirements: technical education in IT, accounting or administration; English at B1 or higher; Excel; clear written communication.

After screening 140 applications, the recruiter **Daniela Paredes** selected two finalists for a 30-minute interview with NorthBridge's support manager, **Emily Chen**.

**Candidate 1: Jorge Mamani**, 23, technical professional in Computer Science from Arequipa. His CV is two pages long, in Spanish format, with a photo, DNI and a list of 14 courses. In the interview, his technical answers were excellent: he explained clearly how he would diagnose a login problem. However, when Emily asked, *"Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult customer,"* he answered: *"I am very patient and I like to help people. Always the clients are happy with me."* He gave no example. When asked about availability, he did not know the time difference between Lima and Toronto.

**Candidate 2: Milagros Flores**, 22, accounting student in her fourth cycle in Lima, with a one-page CV in English and quantified bullets: *"Processed 200+ supplier invoices per month during a six-month internship"*. Her grammar had more errors than Jorge's, and she asked Emily to repeat two questions. But she answered the behavioral question with a clear STAR story about solving an invoice error for an angry supplier, mentioned NorthBridge's new invoicing feature and asked, *"How do you measure success for this role in the first three months?"*

Emily told Daniela: *"Jorge is technically stronger, but I'm not sure he can handle written tickets and customers. Milagros communicates better, but she has less IT background. I need someone who can start in four weeks."*

Daniela has an incentive to close the position quickly, but also a long-term relationship with NorthBridge, which plans to hire 15 more people in Peru next year. She can recommend one candidate, recommend both for a paid one-week trial, or offer Jorge two weeks of interview coaching and a second interview.
questions: Compare the two candidates using the criteria of this unit: CV conventions, STAR answers, questions for the interviewer and practical information.
Rewrite Jorge's answer to the behavioral question as a 100-word STAR story, inventing a plausible situation from his studies.
Which recommendation should Daniela make? Consider NorthBridge's needs, the timeline and her long-term relationship with the client.
What three changes should Jorge make to his CV before applying to an international company? Justify each one.

assignment.title: Proyecto final: portafolio profesional bilingüe y entrevista simulada
assignment.instructions:
**Objetivo:** integrar las competencias del curso en un portafolio profesional que puedas usar para postular a prácticas preprofesionales o empleos con requisito de inglés.

**Qué entregar:**

1. **Oferta laboral seleccionada:** una oferta real de nivel junior o practicante en inglés relacionada con tu carrera (adjunta el texto, sin datos personales de terceros).
2. **CV en inglés** (una página), en orden cronológico inverso, con perfil, verbos de acción, al menos tres logros cuantificados (académicos, laborales o de voluntariado) y nivel de idioma según el MCER.
3. **Carta de presentación** (200 a 280 palabras) en cuatro párrafos, personalizada para la oferta.
4. **Presentación grabada de 3 minutos** sobre un proceso o proyecto de tu carrera, con 4 a 6 diapositivas, secuenciadores, al menos dos oraciones en voz pasiva y la descripción de un gráfico o dato.
5. **Entrevista simulada en vivo** (10 minutos) con el docente en la semana 15, que incluye la pregunta ‘Tell me about yourself’, una pregunta conductual (respuesta STAR) y tus preguntas al entrevistador.
6. **Reflexión final en español** (150 a 200 palabras) comparando tu grabación de la semana 1 con la actual y tu avance en los descriptores del MCER.

**Formato:** un solo PDF con enlaces internos a los videos; sustentación en vivo según cronograma.

**Criterios:** rúbrica adjunta.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses the present simple passive to describe a step in a process?
options: The invoice is send to the client by email.
The invoice is sent to the client by email.
The invoice sent to the client by email.
The invoice is sending to the client by email.
questions.explanation: La pasiva se forma con ‘is’ más participio; el participio de ‘send’ es ‘sent’. Las demás omiten el auxiliar o usan formas incorrectas.

questions.prompt: You started working at a company in 2024 and you still work there. Which sentence is correct?
options: I work here since 2024.
I am working here since 2024.
I've worked here since 2024.
I worked here for 2024.
questions.explanation: Para una situación que empezó en el pasado y continúa se usa presente perfecto con ‘since’ y el punto de inicio.

questions.prompt: In a STAR answer, which part should usually be the longest and most detailed?
options: Situation
Task
Action
Result
questions.explanation: La acción muestra lo que hizo el candidato y sus competencias; situación y tarea deben ser breves, y el resultado concreto.

questions.prompt: Which CV bullet point is most effective for an international employer?
options: Responsible for social media.
I was in charge of many things in the marketing area.
Increased Instagram engagement by 40% in six months by planning weekly video content.
Very good in social media and creative.
questions.explanation: Empieza con verbo de acción, cuantifica el logro e indica cómo se obtuvo; las otras describen funciones vagas o adjetivos.

questions.prompt: A client asks a question about a figure you don't have during your presentation. What is the best response?
options: Give an approximate number to avoid silence.
Say ‘That's not important’ and continue.
Say ‘I don't have that figure now, but I'll check and send it to you today.’
Ignore the question and move to the next slide.
questions.explanation: Reconocer que no se tiene el dato y comprometerse a enviarlo con un plazo es honesto y profesional; inventar cifras es riesgoso.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best introduces and interprets a chart in a presentation?
options: Here is a chart with many numbers.
This chart shows support tickets in 2025. As you can see, they dropped by 35% after the portal launch, so the team has more time for complex cases.
The chart is blue and green and has twelve months.
I will read all the numbers in the chart now.
questions.explanation: Presenta el gráfico, destaca el dato clave e interpreta su implicancia, siguiendo la secuencia de tres pasos de la unidad.

questions.prompt: At the end of an interview, the recruiter asks: ‘Do you have any questions for us?’ What is the best answer?
options: No, thank you, everything is clear.
How many vacation days do I get in the first month?
How do you measure success in this role in the first three months?
What does your company do?
questions.explanation: Una pregunta sobre criterios de éxito muestra interés y orientación a resultados; preguntar qué hace la empresa revela falta de investigación.
